newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Italian sales boost European car market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italian sales boost European car market.

text.p: West European car sales soared nine percent year-on-year in June, partly reflecting a booming Italian market triggered by an incentive scheme, the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) said on Tuesday.
"This nine percent is due to some special effects...and some countries are recovering," said Jorg Schroder, ACEA director of trade and economics.
In the first six months of the year, new car registrations rose a more modest 1.7 percent to 6,991,700.
Asked whether ACEA might revise upwards its forecast of sales growth of more than two percent for the full year, Schroder said: "I hope so."
The increase in new registrations to 1,135,600 cars in June from 1,042,000 the same month last year came after a year-on-year decline of 1.9 percent in May.

In June, Italy stood out with a 50.7 percent jump in registrations to 222,800 cars following a year-on-year increase of 43.2 percent in May, thanks to a national cash incentive scheme which encourages motorists to turn in old cars for scrap in exchange for buying new models.
The scheme was introduced in January.
In contrast, the French market declined 30.7 percent to 93,200 units, still depressed by the end of a similar incentive scheme in France more than six months ago.
Other national markets also showed wide variations.
The Danish market declined 39.5 percent to 7,800 units while the Austrian market rose by 31 percent to 26,600 and the Swedish market by 22.9 percent to 20,900 units.
Germany, the largest car market in Europe, recovered by 8.4 percent to 343,000 after a decline of 12.9 percent in May.
Among car makers, Fiat sales jumped 25.1 percent to 146,000, making it the second largest group in Europe after Germany's Volkswagen, whose sales rose 10.8 percent to 213,200 units.
As a result, Fiat's market share rose to 12.9 percent from 11.2 percent in June last year, still far behind Volkswagen's 18.8 percent share.
Japanese and Korean car makers also strengthened their positions, increasing sales by 15.3 and 23.8 percent respectively.
U.S. giant General Motors lost market share, to 12.3 percent from 13.0 percent, despite a rise in sales of 3.5 percent from last year.
The Ford group, however, increased its share to 11.9 from 11.5 percent as a result of a 12.9 percent increase in sales.
In contrast, France's Renault saw its sales fall 5.1 percent to 95,985 and its market share decrease to 8.5 percent from 9.7 percent.
The ACEA figures include the 15-nation EU, Norway, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
